title: W
full_review:
Much like "The Queen," 2006's cinematic portrait of England's present monarch, with its award-winning central performance by Helen Mirren, Oliver Stone's biography of George W. Bush -- its subject still ensconced in the White House -- "W." (Lionsgate) is largely speculative.

Still, this is a generally absorbing dramatization of a unique president, and he's embodied by Josh Brolin with uncanny accuracy. He seems to have inherited dad James Brolin's unique talent for impersonation -- one that goes beyond mimicry, as witness the elder Brolin's stunning cinematic takes on Ronald Reagan and Clark Gable.

"W." focuses mainly on Bush's decision to invade Iraq and the aftermath of that decision, interspersed with flashbacks showing his undisciplined youth, initiation at Yale, courtship of wife Laura (Elizabeth Banks), and unlikely rise to the governorship of Texas and the presidency.

In fashioning a film that's neither definitive history nor "Saturday Night Live" spoof, director Oliver Stone and screenwriter Stanley Weiser have taken a cautious, surprisingly balanced approach to their central character, and avoided caricature, though certainly not ignoring flaws. Still, if they show us Bush making a grammatical gaffe or some naive declaration -- "Is our children learning?" he remarks to a reporter who questions his views on education, or "If I have to read the whole Constitution, I will," as he declares to Karl Rove (Toby Jones) -- the moment passes without undue emphasis.

Overall, Bush is drawn as a genuinely God-fearing leader whose actions on the international scene stemmed from a rather simplistic sense of good and evil, coming from his born-again conversion at age 40 under the guidance of Earle Hudd (Stacy Keach). Thereafter, he would have his staff lower their heads while he prayed fervently after each staff meeting.

The script contends that the other driving force in his rise on the political ladder was rooted in his complicated relationship with his father, George H. W. Bush (James Cromwell), who, it seemed to W., always favored brother Jeb (Jason Ritter). Both George Sr., and mother Barbara (Ellen Burstyn) are shown to be incredulous upon learning of W.'s plan to run for Texas governor at the same time Jeb was seeking the same position in Florida -- and even more so when W. won and Jeb lost. The strained father-son dynamic becomes more pronounced as the film unwinds.

A host of other familiar personages -- Dick Cheney (Richard Dreyfuss), Condoleezza Rice (Thandie Newton), Colin Powell (Jeffrey Wright), Donald Rumsfeld (Scott Glenn) and Ari Fleischer (Rob Corddry) -- are portrayed as we know them from their public utterances, and in some cases even the physical resemblances are remarkable.

The film contains one use of the F-word, several crude words and brief profanity, a few sexual references, strong but fleeting war footage and alcohol abuse; it is acceptable for older teens. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
